cards.front: Why is there no single perfect diet for everyone?
cards.back: Human metabolism, gut microbiome composition, food preferences, cultural backgrounds and practical constraints vary enormously between individuals. The ZOE project (Tim Spector's large-scale microbiome research) found that identical foods produce dramatically different blood sugar and fat responses in different people. The best diet is the one built from evidence-based principles but adapted to your specific body, lifestyle, tastes and circumstances.

cards.front: What are the non-negotiable nutrition fundamentals — the things that benefit virtually everyone?
cards.back: Despite individual variation, several principles hold across populations: 1) Eat mostly whole, minimally processed food. 2) Eat abundant vegetables and fruits. 3) Eat adequate protein (especially over 50). 4) Stay well hydrated. 5) Minimise ultra-processed food and refined sugar. 6) Eat oily fish or ensure omega-3 intake. 7) Limit alcohol. 8) Avoid smoking. These fundamentals, applied consistently, cover 90% of what nutrition science has to offer.

cards.front: How do you design a personal nutrition approach?
cards.back: Start with the fundamentals, then personalise. Ask: What are my main health goals (energy, weight, longevity, performance)? What foods do I genuinely enjoy? What are my practical constraints (time, budget, cooking ability, cultural context)? What dietary patterns does my family history suggest are important? Build habits around these realities, not an idealised version of yourself. A 70% adherence to a good diet beats 30% adherence to a perfect one.

cards.front: What is the role of experimentation in personal nutrition?
cards.back: Nutrition science gives population-level findings, but you are an individual. Experimentation — trying an eating window, eliminating a suspected trigger food, adding a new whole food — teaches you how your body specifically responds. Keep a simple food and energy journal for 2–3 weeks after any change to notice patterns. Your own data from your own body is the most valuable nutritional information you have.

cards.front: What is the most important mindset for lifelong good nutrition?
cards.back: Progress, not perfection. Nutrition is a practice maintained over decades, not a problem to solve once. Your approach will evolve as your life, body and knowledge change. Missing a week, going through a stressful period or eating poorly on holiday doesn't erase your progress — it's a normal part of a long-term practice. The goal is a sustainable, enjoyable way of eating that supports your life rather than controlling it. That's what eating well for life actually looks like.

quiz.question: What did Tim Spector's ZOE research project find about individual responses to identical foods?
options: Everyone responds to food in the same way
Identical foods produce dramatically different blood sugar and fat responses in different people
Diet does not affect blood sugar significantly
Only genetics determines how food is metabolised
quiz.explanation: The ZOE study — one of the largest nutrition microbiome studies ever conducted — found enormous individual variation in how people respond to identical foods. Blood sugar and fat responses varied dramatically based on individual gut microbiome, genetics and lifestyle, supporting the case for personalised nutrition.

quiz.question: Which of the following is one of the universal nutrition fundamentals that benefits virtually everyone?
options: Eating mostly whole, minimally processed food
quiz.explanation: Eating mostly whole, minimally processed food is one of the most robustly supported nutrition principles across all populations and dietary philosophies. It underpins the Mediterranean diet, plant-based approaches, and virtually every evidence-based longevity dietary pattern.

quiz.question: What is the most important mindset for maintaining good nutrition over a lifetime?
options: Progress over perfection — a sustainable practice maintained consistently over decades
Following the same diet forever without adaptation
quiz.explanation: Lifelong good nutrition is a practice, not a perfect state. Research on long-term healthy eaters shows they focus on consistent patterns rather than perfection, adapt their approach as life changes, recover quickly from setbacks, and prioritise enjoyment alongside health — making it sustainable for decades.
